findings.title: AI-Generated Market Manipulation via Social Media Bots
findings.description:
Using AI-generated text and automated social media bots to create fake hype around microcap stocks, driving up prices before insiders sell their shares (pump-and-dump). The AI models generated realistic-looking posts, news articles, and even fake analyst reports to manipulate retail investor sentiment.

Evasion: 1) Used decentralized VPNs and rotating IP addresses to avoid bot detection. 2) Employed natural language generation (NLG) models to create varied, human-like content. 3) Spread activity across multiple platforms (Twitter, Reddit, Discord, Telegram) to avoid centralized detection. 4) Used burner accounts with aged profiles purchased on darknet markets.
tags: Unusual trading volume spikes in low-liquidity stocks
Correlation between social media activity and price movements without fundamental news
Identical or near-identical language across multiple accounts
Accounts with no prior history suddenly posting about obscure stocks
Rapid account creation and deletion patterns
Suspicious IP address clusters

findings.title: SPAC Fraud with Misleading Projections
findings.description:
Special Purpose Acquisition Companies (SPACs) made wildly optimistic financial projections about target companies, knowing they were unattainable. Executives used complex financial models with unrealistic assumptions to justify valuations, while hiding risks from investors. Some SPACs also engaged in 'SPAC arbitrage' by manipulating the timing of mergers to benefit insiders.

Evasion: 1) Buried key risks in dense legal disclosures. 2) Used complex financial jargon to obscure unrealistic assumptions. 3) Obtained 'independent' third-party valuations that were actually conflicted. 4) Structured deals to avoid traditional IPO scrutiny. 5) Used multiple shell companies to obscure beneficial ownership.
tags: Projections significantly outpacing industry growth rates
Lack of clear path to profitability
Conflicted third-party advisors
Executives with history of failed ventures
Unusual timing of insider stock sales
Overly complex corporate structures

findings.title: NFT Wash Trading for Artificial Valuation
findings.description:
Crypto platforms and NFT marketplaces engaged in wash trading - where the same entity buys and sells NFTs to create artificial trading volume and inflate prices. Some platforms offered incentives for users to engage in wash trading, while others used automated bots to execute trades between controlled accounts. This created the illusion of demand and liquidity.

Evasion: 1) Used multiple crypto wallets with different addresses but common ownership. 2) Spread trades across different exchanges to avoid single-platform detection. 3) Used mixers/tumblers to obscure transaction trails. 4) Executed trades in small increments to avoid large transaction flags. 5) Created fake user accounts with synthetic identities.
tags: Unusual trading patterns (same price, same time, same assets)
High volume with little price movement
Multiple accounts trading the same NFTs in circular patterns
Accounts with no other activity suddenly trading high volumes
Suspicious transaction timing patterns
Use of privacy coins or mixers in funding transactions

findings.title: DeFi Protocol Manipulation via Flash Loans
findings.description:
Exploiting decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols by using flash loans to manipulate token prices, exploit oracle vulnerabilities, and trigger liquidations. Attackers would borrow large sums via flash loans, manipulate the price of a token on one exchange, then use that manipulated price to trigger liquidations or exploit arbitrage opportunities on other protocols before repaying the loan in the same transaction.

Evasion: 1) Executed entire attack in a single blockchain transaction. 2) Used multiple DeFi protocols in sequence to obscure the attack path. 3) Created custom smart contracts to automate the attack. 4) Used privacy-focused blockchains for initial funding. 5) Timed attacks during periods of low liquidity to maximize impact.
tags: Unusual price movements in low-liquidity tokens
Large flash loan transactions immediately followed by liquidations
Smart contract interactions with unusual complexity
Rapid sequence of transactions across multiple protocols
Funding from privacy-focused wallets
Timing of attacks during off-peak hours

findings.title: Insider Trading with Encrypted Messaging Apps
findings.description:
Corporate insiders used encrypted messaging apps (Signal, Telegram, WhatsApp) to share material non-public information (MNPI) about upcoming earnings, mergers, or regulatory decisions. The information was then used to make profitable trades before public disclosure. Some groups created private channels with strict membership controls to limit exposure.

Evasion: 1) Used end-to-end encrypted messaging apps. 2) Created private groups with invitation-only access. 3) Used coded language and emojis to discuss sensitive information. 4) Regularly deleted messages and used ephemeral messaging features. 5) Used burner phones and SIM cards for communication. 6) Conducted in-person meetings to discuss sensitive topics.
tags: Unusual trading patterns before major announcements
Connected individuals trading the same securities in similar patterns
Use of personal devices for work communications
Suspicious timing of message deletions
Employees with sudden unexplained wealth
Unusual travel patterns for in-person meetings

findings.title: Crypto Pump-and-Dump with Influencer Coordination
findings.description:
Organized groups coordinated pump-and-dump schemes for low-cap cryptocurrencies by: 1) Accumulating a large position in a low-liquidity token, 2) Using social media influencers to promote the token to retail investors, 3) Creating artificial trading volume through wash trading, and 4) Selling their holdings at the peak to unsuspecting buyers.

Evasion: 1) Used multiple exchange accounts to accumulate positions. 2) Coordinated influencer promotions through private Telegram groups. 3) Used mixers to obscure fund flows. 4) Created fake trading volume through automated bots. 5) Used decentralized exchanges to avoid KYC requirements. 6) Timed promotions to coincide with natural market volatility.
tags: Sudden price spikes in low-cap tokens with no fundamental news
Correlation between influencer promotions and price movements
Unusual trading volume patterns
Multiple accounts trading the same token in similar patterns
Use of privacy coins in funding transactions
Suspicious wallet clustering

findings.title: Forced Labor in Supply Chains via Fake Labor Contractors
findings.description:
Exploitation of H-2A visa program through shell labor contracting companies. Workers are recruited with false promises of high wages and legal status, then subjected to debt bondage, wage theft, and threats of deportation. Contractors charge exorbitant recruitment fees, confiscate passports, and force workers into substandard housing and dangerous conditions.

Evasion: Layered subcontracting obscures the link between the legitimate agricultural business and the exploitative labor practices. Fake invoices and payroll records are created to show compliance with labor laws. Workers are coached to lie during inspections or audits.
tags: Workers living in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions near worksites
Discrepancies between payroll records and actual hours worked
High recruitment fees reported by workers
Frequent turnover of labor contractors
Workers lacking access to their passports or visas
Unusual deductions from wages (e.g., for housing, tools, or transportation)

findings.title: Online Recruitment Exploitation via Fake Job Ads
findings.description:
Traffickers pose as legitimate employers on social media, job boards, and dating apps to recruit victims for fake job opportunities. Victims are lured with promises of modeling gigs, high-paying jobs, or romantic relationships, then trafficked for forced labor or sex work. Fake websites and contracts are used to appear legitimate.

Evasion: Use of encrypted messaging apps (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram) to communicate with victims. Fake online personas and burner phones avoid traceability. Victims are isolated from support networks and coerced into compliance through threats or violence.
tags: Job ads with vague descriptions or unrealistic pay
Recruiters requesting payment for job placement or visas
Employers communicating primarily via encrypted apps
Victims reporting sudden isolation from family or friends
Inconsistencies in employer details (e.g., fake addresses, untraceable companies)

findings.title: Cryptocurrency-Enabled Human Trafficking
findings.description:
Traffickers use cryptocurrency to pay for online ads, recruiters, and operational expenses. Victims are forced to engage in sex work or forced labor, and their earnings are collected in cryptocurrency. Mixers and privacy coins (e.g., Monero) are used to launder proceeds and obscure transaction trails.

Evasion: Use of decentralized exchanges (DEXs) and peer-to-peer (P2P) platforms to convert cryptocurrency to fiat without KYC checks. Multiple wallets and mixing services (e.g., Tornado Cash) are used to break the transaction trail. Fake identities are used to create accounts on exchanges.
tags: Frequent small cryptocurrency transactions to privacy-focused wallets
Use of mixing services or privacy coins
Victims reporting payment in cryptocurrency
Online ads for trafficking services paid in cryptocurrency
Unusual patterns in blockchain transactions (e.g., rapid movement between wallets)

findings.title: FCPA Violations via Third-Party Labor Brokers
findings.description:
Multinational corporations use third-party labor brokers to source workers for overseas operations. The brokers bribe foreign officials to secure work visas, permits, or favorable treatment for the workers. The corporations claim ignorance of the bribes while benefiting from the corrupt arrangements.

Evasion: Bribes are disguised as 'consulting fees,' 'facilitation payments,' or 'commissions' in contracts with labor brokers. Shell companies or intermediaries are used to obscure the true nature of the payments. Internal controls are bypassed through vague invoices or misclassified expenses.
tags: Unusually high fees paid to labor brokers
Labor brokers with close ties to foreign officials
Frequent use of shell companies or intermediaries in contracts
Inconsistent or vague invoices for services rendered
Workers reporting that they were required to pay bribes for visas or permits
related_indicators: Use of intermediaries to obscure payments

findings.title: Visa Fraud for Exploitation in Tech Outsourcing
findings.description:
Tech staffing companies file fraudulent H-1B visa applications for foreign workers, misrepresenting their job roles, salaries, or work locations. Workers are then placed at client sites under exploitative conditions, such as unpaid overtime, wage theft, or threats of visa revocation if they complain.

Evasion: Fraudulent job descriptions and salary levels are submitted to USCIS to increase the likelihood of visa approval. Workers are coached to lie during visa interviews. Once in the U.S., workers are moved between client sites to avoid detection, and payroll records are falsified to show compliance with labor laws.
tags: Discrepancies between H-1B petitions and actual job roles
Workers reporting unpaid wages or excessive hours
Frequent changes in work locations or client sites
Workers living in overcrowded housing provided by employers
High turnover or sudden departures of workers

findings.title: Money Laundering via Fake Charities for Trafficking Proceeds
findings.description:
Traffickers establish fake charities or nonprofits to launder proceeds from forced labor or sex trafficking. Donations are solicited from the public, and trafficking proceeds are commingled with legitimate funds. The charities may also be used to recruit victims under the guise of 'humanitarian work.'

Evasion: Fake donation receipts and financial records are created to show compliance with nonprofit regulations. Shell companies or intermediaries are used to obscure the source of funds. Charities are dissolved or rebranded frequently to avoid scrutiny.
tags: Charities with no clear mission or vague financial records
High overhead costs or unexplained expenses
Frequent changes in charity leadership or structure
Workers or victims reporting coercion under the guise of 'volunteering'
Unusual cash deposits or wire transfers from unrelated entities

findings.title: H-2A Visa Fraud with Debt Bondage in Agriculture
findings.description:
Recruiters charged exorbitant fees to foreign workers for H-2A visas, then forced them into debt bondage by withholding wages, confiscating passports, and threatening deportation. Workers were housed in substandard conditions and paid below minimum wage, with deductions for 'housing' and 'transportation' that left them with little to no take-home pay.

Evasion: Used shell companies to sponsor H-2A visas, rotated workers between farms to avoid detection by DOL inspectors, and falsified payroll records to show compliance with wage laws. Recruiters operated in workers' home countries (e.g., Mexico, Guatemala) where oversight was minimal, and workers were coached to lie about conditions if questioned by authorities.
tags: Workers living in overcrowded, unsanitary housing (e.g., trailers, barns)
Pay stubs showing excessive deductions for 'fees' or 'housing'
Workers lacking access to their passports or visas
High turnover of workers at specific farms
Recruiters demanding upfront fees for job placement
Inconsistencies in payroll records (e.g., hours worked vs. hours paid)

findings.title: Staffing Agency Labor Trafficking in Food Processing
findings.description:
A staffing agency recruited foreign workers (including undocumented individuals) for food processing plants, then subjected them to forced labor by threatening to report them to ICE if they complained. Workers were forced to work 12+ hour shifts without overtime pay, housed in overcrowded apartments with excessive rent deductions, and paid in cash to avoid payroll taxes.

Evasion: Used multiple staffing agencies as intermediaries to obscure the chain of command, paid workers partially in cash to avoid payroll records, and rotated workers between plants to prevent them from forming relationships with local advocates. The agency also falsified I-9 forms and used fake Social Security numbers to avoid detection by ICE.
tags: Workers paid in cash or with prepaid debit cards
No overtime pay despite long hours
Workers living in overcrowded, substandard housing
High turnover of workers at specific plants
Staffing agencies with no permanent address or online presence
Workers expressing fear of deportation or retaliation
related_indicators: Threats of deportation or other penalties

findings.title: Domestic Servitude via A-3/J-1 Visas
findings.description:
Diplomats or wealthy individuals sponsored domestic workers (e.g., nannies, housekeepers) on A-3 or J-1 visas, then subjected them to forced labor by confiscating their passports, restricting their movement, and threatening them with deportation. Workers were paid little to no wages, forced to work excessive hours, and subjected to verbal or physical abuse. Some were trafficked between multiple households to avoid detection.

Evasion: Exploited diplomatic immunity to avoid prosecution, used private residences to isolate workers from outside contact, and rotated workers between households to prevent them from forming relationships with local communities. Workers were often recruited from their home countries (e.g., Philippines, India) with false promises of fair wages and good working conditions.
tags: Domestic workers rarely seen outside the residence
Workers lacking access to their passports or visas
Signs of physical or verbal abuse (e.g., bruises, fearfulness)
Workers working excessive hours with no days off
No written employment contract or records of wages paid
Workers expressing fear of their employer or deportation
related_indicators: Threats of deportation or other penalties

findings.title: Forced Labor in Supply Chains (UFLPA Enforcement)
findings.description:
A U.S. importer sourced seafood from suppliers in Southeast Asia (e.g., Thailand, Taiwan) that used forced labor in their processing facilities. Workers were recruited with false promises of high wages, then subjected to debt bondage through recruitment fees, forced to work excessive hours, and housed in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions. The importer falsified customs documents to obscure the origin of the goods and avoid UFLPA enforcement.

Evasion: Used multiple layers of suppliers and subcontractors to obscure the supply chain, falsified bills of lading and certificates of origin to misrepresent the source of the goods, and pressured workers to lie about conditions if audited. The importer also relied on third-party audits that were easily manipulated (e.g., staged inspections, coached workers).
tags: Goods sourced from high-risk regions (e.g., Xinjiang, Southeast Asia) with no transparency in the supply chain
Suppliers with a history of labor violations or ties to forced labor
Inconsistencies in customs documentation (e.g., bills of lading, certificates of origin)
Workers at supplier facilities lacking access to passports or wages
High turnover or excessive working hours at supplier facilities
Suppliers refusing to allow unannounced audits or worker interviews

findings.title: Fake H-2B Visa Sponsorship for Non-Existent Jobs
findings.description:
A fraudulent staffing agency filed H-2B visa petitions for non-existent landscaping or hospitality jobs, then charged foreign workers (e.g., from Mexico, Central America) exorbitant fees for the visas. Once in the U.S., workers were abandoned without jobs, forced into exploitative work arrangements (e.g., day labor, construction), or trafficked into other industries. The agency pocketed the fees and disappeared before authorities could investigate.

Evasion: Used shell companies to file visa petitions, rotated between different legal representatives to avoid scrutiny, and targeted workers in rural or underserved areas where oversight was minimal. The agency also coached workers to lie about their job duties and wages if questioned by DOL or ICE investigators.
tags: Staffing agencies with no verifiable business address or online presence
H-2B petitions filed for jobs with vague or inconsistent descriptions
Workers reporting that promised jobs do not exist
High fees charged to workers for visa processing
Workers abandoned at bus stations or airports upon arrival in the U.S.
Multiple H-2B petitions filed by the same agency for the same job type in different locations

findings.title: Forced Labor in Domestic Work via Au Pair Programs
findings.description:
A cultural exchange agency placed au pairs (on J-1 visas) with host families, then failed to monitor their working conditions. Some host families subjected au pairs to forced labor by requiring them to work excessive hours (e.g., 80+ hours per week), paying them below minimum wage, and restricting their movement. The agency ignored complaints from au pairs and threatened them with deportation if they reported abuse.

Evasion: Exploited the cultural exchange aspect of the J-1 visa to avoid labor law enforcement, used private homes to isolate au pairs from oversight, and pressured au pairs to sign non-disclosure agreements. The agency also falsified records to show compliance with program requirements (e.g., hours worked, wages paid).
tags: Au pairs working excessive hours with no days off
Au pairs paid below minimum wage or with no pay stubs
Au pairs expressing fear of their host family or the agency
Au pairs lacking access to their passports or visas
Host families refusing to allow au pairs to attend cultural events or classes
Agencies ignoring or dismissing complaints from au pairs
related_indicators: Threats of deportation or other penalties
